title: Hiring trumpeter Al Blanco and the Donaldsonville Fair
summary: He tells how he heard Blanco at a jam session, took him on, and played the Donaldsonville Fair for Huey Long.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Natural born musician, but he didn't need it. People had money. And they had a jam session. And I had a chance to get a load of Blanco and Pons. And I was delighted. So I said, Blanco, do you know who I am? He says, I believe you're Johnny DeGroote. I said, I am. He said, Mr. DeGroote, I'm so happy to meet you. I said, I don't need a lamp. I said, but I do need a trumpet player. Will you play with me? He almost fainted. I can't. I don't raise your bed. I said, that's for me to judge. So I took him on. And he come on and down with a little bit of bass and trumpet. It's one of the finest made, but cornet. And the week after that we had the Donaldsonville Fair. I brought to the band. We had caps on. We had caps on. We had white suits with black ties. But you know, in the military. I had a fellow on Ramport Street make me some caps. And I played the, all we had to play was the Overture. And Urie Long was in power then. So naturally it was every man a king. We played chorus of every man a king. That was the Overture. Easiest Overture I ever got by. I had a fellow from his name was Hickey from years ago. I don't know, he used to call us, ha ha ha, Hickey, on the radio. He acted as I.M.C. and he'd introduce me with a lot of flowery words and what would I play? I would call us a, but I played the show like they had never had it played before. We had the Blondin' Realms from Pornham and Bailey Six, German, we had acrobats. And of course they were out in the field and we were up in the grandstand. So knowing they were German I played Under the Double Eagle March. I had my books full of stuff because I never knew what I was going to run into. And they'd come out and they'd be boom, oh, they'd straighten up like Germans. And they'd watch them and when they'd start to pull them stuff I'd go up into a Strauss Balls. Those fellas want to kiss me. I said, well they're recording, you're going to have it, they haven't recorded. Give it to the next man, tell them the player don't record it. And then I'd take them down and when they'd come down to the bar, I'd play a gallop while they'd slide them down. You know you've got to wait until they'd come down one at a time. I'd play a gallop and when they'd face the audience I'd give them a big chord and I'd march them off to boom, boom, boom, boom. Oh boy, they'd wish they could carry me around. I said this is far enough. The job was so easy that we could come home every night if it felt like it. I'd get the quarter of the night fair. But I enjoyed it.
